item.title: Kernel Methods for DNA Binding-Site Prediction
item.description:
The challenge

Transcription factors (TFs) regulate gene expression by binding to specific regions of the genome. In this Kaggle data challenge, the final project of the Kernel Methods course at the African Master’s in Machine Intelligence (AMMI), the task was to predict whether a DNA sequence region is a binding site for a given TF.

  • 3 datasets, each with 2,000 labelled training sequences and 1,000 test sequences.
  • One binary classifier per dataset.
  • Goal of the course project: implement the algorithms ourselves and adapt them to structured (sequence) data.

What we did

We started with standard baselines, then moved to kernels designed for sequence data:

  • Hard- and soft-margin SVMs
  • Kernel Logistic Regression and Kernel Ridge Regression with linear, polynomial and RBF kernels
  • Spectrum and mismatch kernels, which compare sequences through their shared k-mers
  • Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL): a combination of k-spectrum kernels with k = 12, 13 and 15, with kernel weights optimised by gradient descent so that the model captures substrings of several lengths at once

Results

Model Public score Private score
Hard-margin SVM 54.61% 54.61%
Soft-margin SVM 53.73% 55.46%
Kernel Logistic Regression 53.46% 53.73%
Kernel Ridge Regression 63.80% 62.90%
Multiple spectrum kernels (MKL) 68.13% 67.00%

Our best model, MKL with spectrum kernels, finished 6th on the private leaderboard. Combining substrings of different lengths proved clearly more effective than any single kernel.

item.title: A comparative study of Bitcoin and Ripple's cryptocurrencies trading using Deep Reinforcement Learning
Understanding Autoencoders & Variational Autoencoders
item.description:
Motivation

Autoencoders (AEs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used for compression, representation learning and generation, yet the effect of their main design choices is often left to trial and error. This project asks a simple question: how do architecture and probabilistic assumptions change what these models learn?

What I did

  • Implemented AE, VAE, VAE with a mean-conditional Gaussian prior and β-VAE models in a single, configurable PyTorch codebase.
  • Ran controlled experiments on three datasets: MNIST, FashionMNIST and FreyFace.
  • Depth sweep: fixed latent dimension $D_z$, varying the number of layers $n_L$.
  • Latent-dimension sweep: fixed depth, varying $D_z$.
  • Prior study: replaced the standard Gaussian prior with a mean-conditional Gaussian prior.
  • β-VAE study: varied $\beta \in \{0.02,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 10\}$ to explore the trade-off between reconstruction quality and latent regularisation.

Outputs

For each configuration, the pipeline produces evaluation metrics, latent-space visualisations, original vs. reconstructed samples, and parameter counts, making it easy to compare models side by side.

item.title: Enhancing Obesity Detection Through SMOTE-based Classification Models: A Comparative Study
Darcy's Law in a 2D Porous Embankment
item.description:
Motivation

Embankments store and channel fresh water, but some water always seeps through them. Knowing how much is key to balancing water conservation against flood risk.

Model

Flow through the porous embankment is described by Darcy’s law:

$$ \mathbf{U} = -\frac{K}{\mu}\left(\nabla p - \rho \mathbf{g}\right), $$

where $K$ is the permeability, $\mu$ the dynamic viscosity, $p$ the pressure and $\rho$ the fluid density. For a horizontal embankment of length $L$ separating two water tables of heights $y_0$ and $y_1$, the steady discharge per unit width is

$$ Q = \frac{K g \left(y_0^2 - y_1^2\right)}{2 \nu L}, $$

with $\nu$ the kinematic viscosity. The analysis is then extended to multilayer embankments (layers of different permeability) and inclined embankments, where gravity acts along the slope.

Results

  • Discharge grows linearly with permeability and decreases with embankment length.
  • Steeper slopes increase the flow.
  • Combining materials of different permeability changes both the total discharge and how water is distributed inside the embankment.
  • Case study (earthfill embankment on impermeable bedrock, two layers): computed discharge $Q \approx 2.68 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, consistent with the theoretical prediction.

item.title: Saltwater Intrusion in Anisotropic Porous Media
item.description:
Motivation

Fresh water makes up less than 3% of the water on Earth, and much of it is stored underground. In coastal aquifers, salt water can push into fresh groundwater, forming a salt wedge that threatens drinking-water supplies.

Question

Most classical salt-wedge results assume an isotropic medium, where permeability is the same in every direction. Real soils are often anisotropic. This thesis asks: how does anisotropic permeability change the position and advance of the freshwater–saltwater interface?

Model and method

Groundwater flow in a 2D vertical section $(x, z)$ of an unconfined aquifer is modelled with a storage equation coupled with Darcy’s law, plus transmission conditions at the freshwater–saltwater interface $\Sigma$:

$$ S\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + \operatorname{div}(\mathbf{U}) = Q^A - Q^P, \qquad \mathbf{U} = -\mathbf{K}\,\nabla h , $$

where $h$ is the hydraulic head, $S$ the storage coefficient, and $Q^A$ and $Q^P$ the recharge and pumping rates. Anisotropy enters through the conductivity tensor

$$ \mathbf{K} = \begin{pmatrix} K_{xx} & 0 \\ 0 & K_{zz} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad K_{xx} = 10\,K_{zz}, $$

since horizontal permeability is typically larger than vertical permeability.

The model was solved with the finite element method in FreeFem++ on a 4 m × 2 m aquifer, simulated over 1,300 days in two scenarios: pumping without recharge and pumping with recharge.

Results

  • Without recharge: the salt wedge advances strongly between days 500 and 700 and loses its oblique shape. From day 1,000, a cone of salt water rises towards the well (upconing). By day 1,300 it approaches the critical point beyond which the aquifer becomes unusable for drinking water.
  • With recharge: the wedge advances much more slowly, and the saltwater cone only appears at day 1,300, about 300 days later than without recharge.
  • Takeaway: recharge (e.g. from rainfall) delays saltwater intrusion, but on its own it is only marginally sufficient to limit the risk under excessive pumping.

Resources

  • 📄 : Influence of the anisotropy of the medium’s permeability on advancing the freshwater–dirty water interface
